title: 5 Ways to Make Rigorous Arguments Fun
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that argumentation, which many assume is dull, can become something students genuinely enjoy, and that it deserves a central place in the curriculum. He grounds the case in Neil Postman and Gerald Graff, who see academia as one big argumentative culture in which every discipline's writing is a form of argument. From a year of teaching ninth graders, he offers five practices: read Graff, teach explicitly that argument pervades life, teach the parts of an argument, share student examples, and hold frequent debates. The move is from theory to a practical, repeatable routine that a teacher can start immediately. His closing emphasis is that debate skill only grows by actually holding debates.
points: Seeing every discipline's writing as a type of argument gives students a unifying frame that carries beyond one classroom.
Students buy in more readily once they notice arguments in ads, family talk and everyday disagreements.
Teach the four parts (claim, reasoning, evidence, respectful handling of naysayers) explicitly and reteach them all year.
Projecting anonymous student paragraphs focuses the class on specific argument skills.
Debates in simple formats, with a rubric and a role for every student, are the way to get better at debating.
quotes: According to Neil Postman, argument forces the arguer to consider the strengths and weaknesses of multiple perspectives (p. 24, CCSS Appendix A). In other words, arguing helps you see the complex nature of things; it gives you the habit of viewing things from many points of view.

In other words, Graff helped me see that a lab report in science and an essay in history and an analysis in psychology and an exposition in English… that all of these pieces of writing, when done well, are simply various types of arguments. They make a claim, and they support that claim with reasoning and evidence.

The immanence of arguments doesn’t end with academia; all of life is pervaded with them. We are passive recipients of arguments (an advertisement argues that you need to buy something; teachers and parents argue about the makings of a good life) and eager participants in arguments (which video game system is the best? what was the best song of Summer 2012?).

An argument begins with a claim. The claim is then explained using reasoning (or a warrant), and it is supported using evidence (or data). It’s also important to know that an effective argument acknowledges and deals with its naysayers.

Perhaps no form of argumentation so perfectly lends itself to teachable moments than the debate. There are endless variations on the types of debates you can hold; I’ve had in-class success with formats no more complex than Lincoln-Douglas and as simple as back-and-forth between two teams.
The key with holding effective debates in class is simply getting started. Having debates is the only way to learn how to make them as lean and mean as they can be in your classroom.
